queue.title: Round 1: propose `a-flow-briefing-names-its-contract` (breaks 2 and 3; F140, F143)
queue.detail: The exploration IS round 1's exploration - do not re-explore, write the proposal. Two defects, one change: (a) `_compose_loop_briefing` (scheduler.py:1732-1833) never names `update_task`, never names a target status, and never uses the word `completed`, so an agent is told 'finish and stop' and is never told what finishing is; (b) `is_review` is computed at scheduler.py:2356-2366 and :2713, passed to `_briefing_checkpoint`, and dropped on the next line, so a reviewer receives the implementation briefing verbatim while the context channel tells it the opposite. Create with `openspec new change a-flow-briefing-names-its-contract` (NO date prefix - archiving applies it; a name starting with a digit is refused). Spec deltas: agent-flows almost certainly needs a new requirement stating what a flow's briefing must tell an implementation turn about finishing, and that a review turn's briefing is review-shaped. Note the corpus silence recorded in the exploration section 5: NO requirement defines what causes in_progress -> completed, so you are adding one, not satisfying one. `openspec validate --strict` must pass.

queue.title: Round 1: propose `a-review-a-flow-cannot-staff-is-named` (break 4; F142)
queue.detail: scheduler.py:1365-1369 drops an unattributable task with a bare `continue` that records nothing - not unstaffed, not deferred, not in_flight, not gated, no log, no event. This BREACHES agent-flows:134's scenario 'WHEN no agent can be resolved or found for a task THEN the operator is notified, naming the task'. So the minimum repair is enforcement, not new design: append to `unstaffed` with a reason naming the task. The deeper half is a judgement: `agent_that_completed` (task_transition_service.py:123-147) does not filter on actor_kind, so an operator's completion returns None, ambiguous with 'nobody completed this', and seven callers read None three different ways. Decide in the proposal whether to disambiguate it (a second function, or a richer return) and whether a flow may staff a review for work the OPERATOR completed - and if so, who counts as the author to exclude. task-lifecycle-governance:313 was written assuming a name is returned and has no clause for None; the exploration section 5 records that as a gap in the requirement, not only in the code.

queue.title: Round 1: propose `approval-refuses-unaccepted-evidence` (breaks 5 and 6; F122) - OPERATOR DECISION D-A
queue.detail: The operator decided on 2026-08-30: approval is REFUSED while evidence sits unaccepted. Rejected alternatives, do not re-propose: seeding a granted agent per project; a flow granting its resolved reviewer per task; leaving the machinery alone and merely surfacing 'approved but unmerged' (rejected because it leaves task-lifecycle-governance:638 breached). THE SCOPING CONSTRAINT IS THE WHOLE DESIGN: refuse only when evidence EXISTS and is unaccepted. A task with no evidence at all must stay approvable or every research, docs and decision task wedges - this is `_check_mergeable`'s own written rule, 'approval must never be blocked by the absence of an integration, only by one that would fail'. Second half of the same change: accepting evidence must trigger integration for an already-approved task waiting on it (spec.py:864-891 and agent_actions.py:1164-1201 currently do not, so the natural repair sequence still merges nothing). Spec deltas: task-lifecycle-governance - a new refusal beside :688, and :720's CLOSED enumeration of when integration cannot be attempted almost certainly needs amending.

Check what the flow does with a refused approval: does the reviewer's turn end cleanly, does the task stay under_review, is that a wedge or a wait? Drive it if reading is not conclusive.

decisions_for_user.question: C: where does the unaccepted-evidence refusal live?
decisions_for_user.pre_authorised_default: In requirement_gate, as a sibling of GateRefusal.unmergeable and on the same rationale - `_check_mergeable`'s docstring already draws exactly this line ('rigor is a claim about how well the work must be proven; this is a claim about whether it can go where approval puts it') and GateRefusal already separates 'this cannot go in' from 'this is unproven'. It MUST be rigor-independent for the same reason _check_mergeable is. Cost if wrong: a refusal in the wrong module, cheap to move while nothing depends on its location.
decisions_for_user.raise_it_if: placing it there forces requirement_gate to import something that creates a cycle, or the refusal needs to fire somewhere apply_transition does not reach.

decisions_for_user.question: C: what exactly counts as 'evidence sits unaccepted'?
decisions_for_user.pre_authorised_default: Evidence rows for this task in review_state 'awaiting'. REJECTED evidence is NOT this case - it has been judged, and refusing on it would wedge a task whose author must now record better evidence. Name every awaiting row in the refusal, not just the count. Cost if wrong: an over- or under-broad refusal, found immediately by DRIVE-1.
decisions_for_user.raise_it_if: the honest predicate needs to distinguish evidence recorded against a requirement this task is not linked to.

decisions_for_user.question: C: a task with SOME accepted evidence naming a commit AND some still awaiting - refuse, or allow?
decisions_for_user.pre_authorised_default: ALLOW. The goal is that approval always merges something when there is something to merge; if accepted evidence already names a commit, integration will merge it and approval keeps its meaning. Refusing here would block work that is genuinely ready because a second piece of evidence is still in review. Record the awaiting rows as an advisory on the transition rather than a refusal. Cost if wrong: a task merges the older of two commits, visible in the integration record and correctable by a retry after acceptance.
decisions_for_user.raise_it_if: round 2 finds that the awaiting evidence routinely names a NEWER commit than the accepted one, which would make allowing it merge stale work.

decisions_for_user.question: D: how does a loop declare whether its work needs evidence, and what is the default?
decisions_for_user.pre_authorised_default: A column on Loop plus a create_loop parameter, defaulting to NOT requiring evidence. Rationale for that default: a loop today can never merge anything at all, so defaulting to evidence-free is what makes the feature work and regresses nothing - no existing loop is landing work that could break. Name it for what it means to the operator, not for the mechanism. Cost if wrong: a default that surprises someone whose loop starts merging; bounded because loop tasks are per-task-isolated branches.
decisions_for_user.raise_it_if: round 2 or 3 finds an existing loop path that DOES merge today, which would make this a behaviour change rather than a new capability.

decisions_for_user.question: D: when a loop needs no evidence, what commit is merged?
decisions_for_user.pre_authorised_default: The task's own branch, agentweave/task/<task_id>, because `work-is-isolated-per-task` guarantees it carries that task's work and nothing else - which is precisely the property F58 was about. VERIFY that guarantee holds for LOOP tasks specifically before relying on it; that change was written about flows. Do NOT merge an agent branch (agentweave/<agent>) - that is F58 exactly, and it ships every task the agent ever touched. Cost if wrong: the F58 class of defect, which is severity A, so verify rather than assume.
decisions_for_user.raise_it_if: loop tasks turn out not to get per-task worktrees, in which case there is no safe branch to merge and this needs the operator.

decisions_for_user.question: The drives will find new defects. Which get fixed unattended and which are merely filed?
decisions_for_user.pre_authorised_default: FIX what is small, self-contained and unambiguous - a wrong status code, a missing field, a message naming the wrong thing - each with a reproduction first and its own commit. FILE anything that needs a design decision, changes a lifecycle, touches a shipped requirement, or has more than one defensible answer. When in doubt, file it: a filed finding costs the operator two minutes to read, a wrong fix costs a spec loop to undo.
decisions_for_user.raise_it_if: a drive finds something severity A that blocks the rest of the run.

decisions_for_user.question: F47/F120 attribution - the flow's own claim is recorded as the operator's. Fix it in this run?
decisions_for_user.pre_authorised_default: NO. Out of scope, and deliberately. task-lifecycle-governance:359 FORBIDS a third actor kind categorically, with a scenario pinning the enumeration, so the obvious repair breaches a shipped requirement and needs the operator. The alternative it blesses - acting AS the responsible run via origin=runtime - needs the claim reordered after run creation, which touches every loop rather than only flows. If B's work makes a narrow attribution fix fall out for free, propose it and STOP; do not implement it.
